title: Solving Right Triangles
learningObjective: Use trigonometric functions and the Pythagorean Theorem to solve right triangles.

faqs.question: What does it mean to "solve" a right triangle?
faqs.answer:
Solving a right triangle means finding every side and angle: three sides and three angles, one of which (the 90° angle) you already know. You usually start with only a couple of the others. Since the triangle has a 90° angle by definition, and its two acute angles must add to 90° (faq-3), you actually only need a small amount of starting information (any two sides, or one side and one acute angle) to figure out everything else. Throughout this page, every triangle is a right triangle with its right angle at vertex C. The triangle can be drawn in any position; the labels are what matter.

Every triangle on this page is a right triangle: the right angle is always at vertex C, and the hypotenuse c is the longest side, directly across from it. "Solving" means finding all six parts — three sides and three angles.

faqs.question: How do I know which trig ratio (sine, cosine, or tangent) to use for a given problem?
faqs.answer:
Identify which two sides — relative to the angle you care about — are actually involved in the problem (the ones you know, plus the one you're solving for), then match that pair to the right ratio using SOH-CAH-TOA.

Right triangle ABC with the right angle at C. Relative to angle A: side a is opposite, side b is adjacent, and side c (the hypotenuse) is always across from the right angle.

SOH-CAH-TOA (relative to angle A)

\( \sin(A) = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{a}{c} \)

\( \cos(A) = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{b}{c} \)

\( \tan(A) = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac{a}{b} \)

If the angle you know is B, the roles switch: b is opposite B, a is adjacent to B, and c is still the hypotenuse.

faqs.question: Why do the two acute angles in a right triangle always add up to 90°?
faqs.answer:
Every triangle's three angles add up to 180° total. Since a right triangle already uses up 90° on its right angle, the remaining two angles have no choice but to split the other 90° between them — whatever isn't used by one acute angle belongs entirely to the other, so each acute angle is strictly between 0° and 90°.

The three angles add to 180°. The right angle at C uses 90°, so the two acute angles A and B share the remaining 90°.

faqs.question: When do I use an inverse trig function versus a regular trig function while solving a triangle?
faqs.answer: Use a regular trig function (sin, cos, tan) when you already know an angle and are solving for a missing SIDE. Use an inverse trig function (PF3's arcsin, arccos, arctan) when you already know two sides and are solving for a missing ANGLE — since the inverse function is exactly the tool that "undoes" the ratio and hands back the angle itself. For inverse sine and inverse cosine, the ratio is a leg over the hypotenuse, so it is always strictly between 0 and 1. If your calculator gives an error, or a ratio bigger than 1, you have put the hypotenuse on top.

faqs.question: How do I find a missing angle when I'm given two sides?
faqs.answer:
Name the two given sides relative to the angle you want (opposite, adjacent, or hypotenuse), write the matching ratio, then use the matching inverse function. Use the Pythagorean Theorem for the third side.

Right triangle ABC (right angle at C) with a = 35 and c = 37 given; b = 12 is found with the Pythagorean Theorem. Angle A is the unknown, found with inverse sine.

Worked Example — right triangle ABC, right angle at C

Given \( a=35 \) and \( c=37 \) (hypotenuse): \( b=\sqrt{37^2-35^2}=12 \). Find angle A.

\( \sin(A)=\dfrac{35}{37} \)

\( A=\arcsin\left(\dfrac{35}{37}\right)\approx 71.1° \)

\( B=90^\circ-71.1^\circ=18.9^\circ \)

faqs.question: How do I find the missing sides when I'm given one angle and the hypotenuse?
faqs.answer:
Use sine to find the side opposite your known angle, and cosine to find the side adjacent to it — both ratios use the hypotenuse directly, so no extra steps are needed.

Right triangle ABC (right angle at C): known angle B = 53° and hypotenuse c = 5 m. Sides a and b (and angle A) are unknown.

Worked Example — right triangle ABC, right angle at C

Triangle ABC: \( B=53° \), \( c=5 \) meters (hypotenuse). Find sides a and b to the nearest tenth, and angle A.

\( \sin(53°)=\dfrac{b}{5} \) → \( b=5\sin(53^\circ)\approx 4.0 \) meters

\( \cos(53°)=\dfrac{a}{5} \) → \( a=5\cos(53^\circ)\approx 3.0 \) meters

\( A=90^\circ-53^\circ=37^\circ \)

faqs.question: How do I find the missing sides when I'm given one angle and one leg (not the hypotenuse)?
faqs.answer:
Use tangent to find the other leg directly (since tangent doesn't involve the hypotenuse at all), then use sine or cosine — or the Pythagorean theorem — to find the hypotenuse afterward.

Right triangle ABC (right angle at C): known angle A = 28° and leg b = 29.3 mi (a leg, not the hypotenuse). Side a, hypotenuse c, and angle B are unknown.

Worked Example — right triangle ABC, right angle at C

Triangle ABC: \( A=28° \), \( b=29.3 \) miles. Find side a, the hypotenuse c, and angle B.

\( \tan(28°)=\dfrac{a}{29.3} \) → \( a=29.3\tan(28°)\approx 15.6 \) miles

\( \cos(28°)=\dfrac{29.3}{c} \) → \( c=\dfrac{29.3}{\cos(28°)}\approx 33.2 \) miles

\( B=90^\circ-28^\circ=62^\circ \)

If you use the Pythagorean Theorem for c, use the unrounded value of a.

faqs.question: How do I decide whether to use a trig ratio or the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side?
faqs.answer: Use the Pythagorean Theorem when you know two of the three sides (given, or found earlier at full precision) and need the third — it doesn't involve angles at all. Use a trig ratio whenever an angle is part of what you know or need, since the Pythagorean theorem has no way to bring an angle measure into the picture.

faqs.question: How do I find the second acute angle once I already know the first one?
faqs.answer:
Subtract the known acute angle from 90° (faq-3) — no trig ratio needed for this step at all, just simple subtraction.

With B = 53° known, the other acute angle needs no trig at all — just subtract from 90°.

Worked Example — right triangle ABC, right angle at C

If \( B=53° \), then \( A=90°-53°=37° \).

faqs.question: How do I round to the correct number of decimal places when solving a triangle?
faqs.answer:
CheckIt always tells you how to round, and it uses two patterns. When the sides are whole numbers (like 8, 15, 17), it asks for sides to the nearest integer and angles to the nearest tenth of a degree. When the angles are whole degrees (like 35°), it asks for sides to the nearest tenth and angles to the nearest degree. Keep full calculator precision through every step, and when you have a choice, compute each answer from the numbers you were given, not from a value you already rounded: rounding a side early and then reusing it can change the last digit of the next answer. For example, with \( A=70^\circ \) and \( b=3.1 \), \( c=\tfrac{3.1}{\cos 70^\circ}\approx 9.06 \), which rounds to 9.1, but \( \sqrt{8.5^{2}+3.1^{2}}\approx 9.05 \) from the rounded \( a=8.5 \) rounds to 9.0. One more CheckIt detail: when it gives you a decimal side like 6.9, that side was already rounded, so occasionally a correct answer differs from the key by one in the last digit. If that happens, show your instructor your work.

Heads-up about CheckIt's answer key: when your CheckIt problem has whole-degree angles (like 25°), its key currently labels side \(a\) as the leg next to angle \(A\) instead of across from it. Solve with the labels used here. Depending on what you are given, the key may show \(a\) and \(b\) swapped (angle and hypotenuse given), \(A\) and \(B\) swapped (two sides given), or different numbers altogether (angle and one leg given). If your work passes the checks (the hypotenuse is the longest side, \(a^2+b^2\approx c^2\), the larger angle is across from the longer leg) but does not match, show your instructor.

faqs.question: How does solving right triangles connect to PF3's inverse trig functions?
faqs.answer: Every "find the missing angle" step in this section is PF3's arcsin, arccos, and arctan put to direct use. In PF3 you found exact values like \( \arcsin\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac{\pi}{6} \) in radians. Here the ratios are ordinary decimals like \( \tfrac{6.9}{12} \), so you use the calculator's \( \sin^{-1} \), \( \cos^{-1} \), \( \tan^{-1} \) keys in degree mode. Because a right triangle's acute angles are strictly between 0° and 90°, the calculator's inverse-function answer is always the angle you want.

faqs.question: How does this connect to TR3's original right-triangle trig definitions?
faqs.answer: TR3 defined sine, cosine, and tangent as ratios of a right triangle's sides in the first place — opposite over hypotenuse, adjacent over hypotenuse, opposite over adjacent. TE4 uses those same ratios in both directions: with an angle and a side you use the ratio to find another side, and with two sides you use the inverse function to find an angle.

faqs.question: Why does solving right triangles matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: This is one of the most widely used skills in trigonometry — surveying, navigation, construction, and physics all rely constantly on finding an unknown side or angle of a right triangle from partial information. It's also the essential foundation for TE5's Law of Sines and Law of Cosines, which extend the same "solve for everything" idea to triangles that aren't right triangles at all. (The applications are beyond the TE4 CheckIt exercise, which asks only for a labeled triangle to solve.)

guided.title: Name the Sides Before You Pick a Ratio
guided.prompt: I'm practicing TE4 in Math 172: solving right triangles where angle C is 90 degrees, side a is across from angle A, side b is across from angle B, and side c is the hypotenuse. Give me one right triangle at a time with one acute angle (a multiple of 5 degrees) and one side given. Sometimes give angle A and sometimes angle B, and sometimes give a leg and sometimes the hypotenuse. For each one, before I calculate anything, I'll tell you which side is opposite the given angle, which is adjacent, which is the hypotenuse, and which ratio (sin, cos, or tan) connects the given side to the side I want. Don't confirm until I explain my choice. Then I'll solve, rounding sides to the nearest tenth. On the third triangle, show me your own setup with one deliberate mistake in it (for example, calling the hypotenuse the adjacent side, or using the angle A labels when the given angle is B) and ask me to find it. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Find the Angles from Two Sides
guided.prompt: I'm practicing TE4 in Math 172: solving a right triangle (angle C is 90 degrees, side a across from angle A, side b across from angle B, hypotenuse c) when I'm given two sides. Give me one triangle at a time. Mix two kinds, like CheckIt does: (1) whole-number sides from a Pythagorean triple, where I round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree, and (2) decimal sides like 6.9 and 12, where I round sides to the nearest tenth and angles to the nearest degree. Mix which two sides you give: both legs, or a leg and the hypotenuse. For each triangle, ask me first whether the missing side is a leg or the hypotenuse, and which ratio I'll use for angle A. Don't do the steps for me; ask one short question at a time. Once in the session, show me a solution with one deliberate mistake (such as adding squares to find a leg, or using inverse tangent with the hypotenuse) and ask me to spot it. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's Solved Triangle
guided.prompt: I'm practicing TE4 in Math 172. CheckIt asks: "Solve the triangle, i.e. find all remaining sides and angles," with angle C = 90 degrees and side a across from angle A. Play a classmate. Give me a right-triangle problem in that style (one angle and one side, or two sides, with CheckIt-style rounding), then show me your complete "solution" with exactly one mistake hidden in it. Choose from: a wrong ratio, a and b swapped, B found as 180 minus A, a rounded value reused in a later step that changes the answer, or radian-mode output. Don't tell me where it is. I'll check your answer by testing it: is the hypotenuse the longest side, is a^2 + b^2 close to c^2, is the larger angle across from the longer leg, and does each step use the given values? Then I'll name the mistake and fix it. Do two rounds, one of each problem type. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Trig Ratio or Pythagorean Theorem?
guided.prompt: I'm practicing TE4 in Math 172: right triangles with angle C = 90 degrees, side a across from angle A, side b across from angle B, hypotenuse c. Give me six short scenarios, one at a time. Some give two sides, some give an angle and a side, and each names the one part I should find next. For each, I'll say which tool I'd use (sine, cosine, tangent, an inverse trig function, the Pythagorean Theorem, or "subtract from 90 degrees") and why, before solving anything. Don't tell me if I'm right until I've explained. For one scenario, ask me whether it is safe to use a side I already rounded in the Pythagorean Theorem, and have me test it with numbers. For another, state a "rule" about when to use the Pythagorean Theorem that is subtly wrong, and ask me whether I agree. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: How TR3 and PF3 Team Up in TE4
guided.prompt: I'm in Math 172. In TR3 I used a right triangle to find sine, cosine, and tangent as ratios of sides. In PF3 I found exact inverse trig values like arcsin(1/2) = pi/6, in radians. Now in TE4 I solve right triangles. Ask me first to describe, in my own words, when a TE4 problem needs a regular trig function and when it needs an inverse one. Then give me two TE4 problems, one of each kind, and ask me to say which earlier skill each step uses. Next, write a four-sentence summary of how TR3 and PF3 combine in TE4, and include one claim that is false (for example, about radians versus degrees, or about the range of the inverse functions). I'll check every claim against my class notes and tell you which one is wrong and why. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

paths.label: TE4: Solving Right Triangles

The stop "Extension: Angles of elevation" goes beyond the TE4 CheckIt exercise and is optional.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews TE4 leans on: triangle labels and SOH-CAH-TOA (TR3), and inverse trig (PF3), now on a calculator in degree mode. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Label the triangle
stops.target: In right triangle \(ABC\) with \(C = 90^\circ\): side \(a\) is across from angle \(A\), side \(b\) is across from angle \(B\), and the hypotenuse \(c\) is across from the right angle. From angle \(A\), side \(a\) is opposite and side \(b\) is adjacent.
stops.cold: From angle \(A\), which side is opposite, which is adjacent, and which is the hypotenuse? From angle \(B\)?[[graph:LBL]]
stops.coldPlain: In right triangle ABC with C = 90 degrees, from angle A which side is opposite, adjacent, and the hypotenuse? From angle B?
stops.coldA: From \(A\): opposite \(a\), adjacent \(b\), hypotenuse \(c\). From \(B\): opposite \(b\), adjacent \(a\), hypotenuse \(c\). Opposite and adjacent swap when you change angles; the hypotenuse never does.
stops.solution: Lowercase letters name the side across from the matching capital-letter angle. Stand at angle A: the side across is a (opposite), the leg touching A is b (adjacent). Stand at B and they swap.
stops.mistake: Calling the hypotenuse "adjacent" because it touches the angle.
stops.again: In a right triangle with \(a = 16\), \(b = 30\), \(c = 34\), find \(\sin A\), \(\cos A\), \(\tan A\), and \(\sin B\).[[graph:T512]]
stops.reflect: Why is \(\sin A\) always equal to \(\cos B\) in a right triangle?

stops.title: Calculator: trig and inverse trig in degrees
stops.target: Make sure your calculator is in degree mode. Use \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\tan\) to go from an angle to a ratio, and \(\sin^{-1}\), \(\cos^{-1}\), \(\tan^{-1}\) to go from a ratio back to an angle.
stops.cold: Find \(\sin 41^\circ\) to four decimals. Then find the angle \(\theta\) with \(\sin\theta = 0.6\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.coldPlain: Find sin 41 degrees to four decimals. Then find theta with sin theta = 0.6, to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.solution: In degree mode, sin(41 degrees) = 0.6561. To undo sine, use inverse sine: sin^(-1)(0.6) is about 36.87, which rounds to 36.9 degrees.
stops.mistake: Leaving the calculator in radian mode (sin 41 would come out about -0.1586).
stops.reflect: How can you tell your calculator is in the wrong mode?

stages.desc: The two kinds of TE4 problem (given an angle and a side, or given two sides), then the full solve. An optional extension applies it to angles of elevation.

stops.title: Missing sides from an angle and a side
stops.target: Pick the ratio that uses the angle you know, the side you know, and the side you want: \(\sin = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}\), \(\cos = \tfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}\), \(\tan = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\). Then solve.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(C = 90^\circ\), \(A = 15^\circ\), and \(c = 13\). Find \(a\), \(b\), and \(B\). Round sides to the nearest tenth.[[graph:T2q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, C = 90 degrees, A = 15 degrees, c = 13. Find a, b, and B. Round sides to the nearest tenth.
stops.note: Show which ratio (sin, cos, or tan) you set up for each missing part and why. Then check the answer: the hypotenuse must be the longest side, a^2 + b^2 should be close to c^2, and the larger acute angle must be across from the longer leg.
stops.coldA:
[[graph:S2]][[graph:T2s]]

CheckIt's key can list \(a\) and \(b\) the other way around for whole-degree problems; see the heads-up in the Practice check.
stops.solution: B = 90 - 15 = 75 degrees. From A, a is opposite and c is the hypotenuse, so sin 15 degrees = a/13 and a = 13 sin 15 degrees, about 3.4. b is adjacent, so cos 15 degrees = b/13 and b is about 12.6. Check: 3.4^2 + 12.6^2 is about 170, close to 13^2 = 169.
stops.mistake: Using tan when the hypotenuse is the known side.
stops.again: \(C = 90^\circ\), \(B = 70^\circ\), and \(a = 4.1\). Find \(b\) and \(c\). Round sides to the nearest tenth.
stops.againA: From \(B\), \(a\) is adjacent. \(\tan 70^\circ = \tfrac{b}{4.1}\), so \(b = 4.1\tan 70^\circ \approx 11.3\). \(\cos 70^\circ = \tfrac{4.1}{c}\), so \(c = \tfrac{4.1}{\cos 70^\circ} \approx 12.0\). (When the unknown is in the denominator, you divide.)
stops.reflect: How do you decide between sin, cos, and tan?

stops.title: Missing angles from two sides
stops.target: With two sides, use the Pythagorean Theorem for the third side and inverse trig for an angle: \(\tan A = \tfrac{a}{b}\) gives \(A = \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{a}{b}\right)\).
stops.cold: \(C = 90^\circ\), \(a = 12\), \(b = 16\). Find \(c\), \(A\), and \(B\). Round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree.[[graph:T3q]]
stops.coldPlain: C = 90 degrees, a = 12, b = 16. Find c, A, and B. Round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.note: Show which ratio (sin, cos, or tan) you set up for each missing part and why. Then check the answer: the hypotenuse must be the longest side, a^2 + b^2 should be close to c^2, and the larger acute angle must be across from the longer leg.
stops.solution: c = sqrt(144 + 256) = sqrt(400) = 20. From A, a = 12 is opposite and b = 16 is adjacent, so tan A = 12/16 and A = tan^(-1)(12/16), about 36.9 degrees. B = 90 - 36.9 = 53.1 degrees.
stops.again: \(C = 90^\circ\), \(a = 9\), \(c = 41\). Find \(b\), \(A\), and \(B\). Round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.reflect: Why do you need an inverse trig function here but not in the previous stop?

stops.title: Solve the whole triangle
stops.target: Solve means find every missing side and angle. A good order: the other acute angle (they add to 90°), then sides with trig or the Pythagorean Theorem, then check.
stops.cold: Solve triangle \(ABC\) with \(C = 90^\circ\), \(A = 70^\circ\), and \(b = 3.1\). Round sides to the nearest tenth.[[graph:T4q]]
stops.coldPlain: Solve triangle ABC with C = 90 degrees, A = 70 degrees, b = 3.1. Round sides to the nearest tenth.
stops.note: Show which ratio (sin, cos, or tan) you set up for each missing part and why. Then check the answer: the hypotenuse must be the longest side, a^2 + b^2 should be close to c^2, and the larger acute angle must be across from the longer leg.
stops.solution: B = 20 degrees. From A, b = 3.1 is adjacent. tan 70 degrees = a/3.1, so a is about 8.5. cos 70 degrees = 3.1/c, so c = 3.1/cos 70 degrees, about 9.1. Check: 8.5^2 + 3.1^2 is about 81.9 and 9.1^2 is about 82.8, close enough for rounded sides. If you had used the rounded a = 8.5 in the Pythagorean Theorem you would get c of about 9.05, which rounds to 9.0: that is why you round only at the end.
stops.mistake: Rounding a early and then using the rounded value to find c.
stops.again: Solve the triangle with \(C = 90^\circ\), \(b = 12\), \(c = 37\). Round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.reflect: How can you check a solved triangle without redoing the work?

stops.title: Extension: Angles of elevation (beyond the TE4 CheckIt exercise)
stops.target: Draw the right triangle hiding in the situation, label what you know, then solve it like any other right triangle.
stops.cold: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall, making a \(72^\circ\) angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
stops.coldPlain: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall, making a 72 degree angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
stops.coldA: The ladder is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the \(72^\circ\) angle: \(h = 20\sin 72^\circ \approx 19.0\) feet.
stops.solution: Sketch: ground, wall, ladder. The ladder (20) is the hypotenuse and the height is opposite the 72 degree angle at the ground, so sin(72 degrees) = h/20 and h is about 19.0 feet.
stops.mistake: Using cos(72 degrees) (that gives the distance from the wall).
stops.again: You stand 80 feet from the base of a 50-foot building. Ignoring your own height, what is the angle of elevation from the ground where you stand to the top of the building? Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.reflect: What is the first thing you do with a word problem like this?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the TE4 CheckIt: solve a right triangle given an angle and a side, and one given two sides.

(2) In triangle \(ABC\), \(C = 90^\circ\), \(a = 10\), and \(b = 24\). Solve the triangle. Round sides to the nearest integer and angles to the nearest tenth of a degree.

stops.coldA:
(1) \(A = 65^\circ\), \(b \approx 5.1\), \(a \approx 10.9\).[[graph:SF1]][[graph:F1s]](2) \(c = 26\), \(A \approx 22.6^\circ\), \(B \approx 67.4^\circ\).[[graph:SF2]][[graph:F2s]]

stops.solution: (1) A = 65 degrees. From B, b is opposite and c the hypotenuse: b = 12 sin(25 degrees), about 5.1; a = 12 cos(25 degrees), about 10.9. (2) c = sqrt(100 + 576) = 26; A = tan^(-1)(10/24), about 22.6 degrees; B = 67.4 degrees.
stops.mistake: Mixing up which side is opposite B versus opposite A. (Also: CheckIt's current answer key labels a and b the other way around when the angles are whole degrees; the solution here uses the standard labels, side a across from angle A.)
stops.again: (1) \(C = 90^\circ\), \(A = 70^\circ\), \(a = 6.5\). Solve the triangle (sides to the nearest tenth). (2) \(C = 90^\circ\), \(a = 9.5\), \(b = 5.5\). Solve the triangle. Round sides to the nearest tenth and angles to the nearest degree.
